Example 3. EU8 national:

started work with the first employer on 1 January 2005, applied to register the employment on the WRS on 15 February and was subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate on 20 February 2005

stopped working with the first employer on 30 July 2005

started work with a second employer on 5 August 2005, applied to register it on the WRS on 20 September and was subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate on 23 September 2005

In this cases, the EU8 national did not complete 12 months legal employment on 1 January 2006 as:

They were legally working at the start of the 12 month period. This is because the first 30 days of employment is considered legal.

They were legally working at the end of the 12 month period. This is because they had registered the second employer who they were working with at the end of the 12 month period, on the WRS.

They had a gap of 30 days or more when they were not working and not in legal employment. This is because:

they applied to register their first employment on the WRS after 30 days of starting (so there is a gap of unlawful employment between the end of the first 30 days that is considered legal employment and the date they were issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate)

they applied to register their second employment on the WRS after 30 days of starting (so there is a gap of unlawful employment between the end of the first 30 days that is considered legal employment and the date they were issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate)

they were not working between 30 July 2005 and 5 August 2005 (so there was a gap when they were not in employment)

the total gap when they were not working and not in legal employment is more than 30 days

The earliest the EU8 national would have completed 12 months legal employment is 20 February 2006 (the date they were issued with the Accession State WRS Registration Certificate for the first job). This is because from this date, the total gap when the EU8 national was not in employment or legal employment was less than 30 days.

For the purpose of Treaty rights passport applications, we can accept periods of employment from 20 February 2005.

EU2 worker: authorisation to work

A transitional arrangement was in place from 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2013 for EU2 nationals who wanted to start work in the UK.

Unless they were exempt, EU2 nationals had to register their employment on the Accession Worker Scheme (AWS) before they started work. When they did, they were issued with an Accession Worker Card (known as a purple card) that gave them permission to work for a named employer only.

If an EU2 national changed employer within the first 12 months, they had to register the new employment on the AWS before starting work. When they registered the new employment on the AWS, they got a new Accession Worker Card.

When an EU2 national completed 12 months legal employment on the AWS, they became exempt from registering further employment on it and could apply for a Registration Certificate (known as a blue card). An EU2 national is considered to have completed 12 months legal employment on the WRS if they met all of the following criteria:

they were in legal employment at the start of the 12 month period - this means they registered their employment on the AWS before they started working with the employer

they were in legal employment at the end of the 12 month period - this means they registered the employer who they were working for at the end of the 12 month period on the AWS, before they started working with them

during the 12 month period, the total number of days they were not working or not in legal employment is not more than 30 days

Before 1 January 2014, an EU2 national who was not exempt from the AWS who worked in line with their Accession Worker Card:

only had a right of residence as a worker

is not considered a worker if they became unemployed (under 6(2) of the EEA Regulations)

Accession Worker Scheme: students who were working

EU2 national students did not need to register on the AWS if they:

worked no more than 20 hours during term-time (they must have a registration certificate (which is yellow) that confirms they are a student with access to the UK labour market for 20 hours per week)

worked full-time during student holidays

were doing work that was part of their course

If an EU2 student wanted to work more than 20 hours per week during term-time, they needed to register their employment on the AWS.

EU2 students could work for up to 4 months after their course ended, as long as they were issued with a valid Registration Certificate while they were studying.

Accession Worker Scheme: exemptions

EU2 nationals did not have to register on the AWS, if they:

exercised their Treaty rights for the full 5 year qualifying period as, a:

self-employed person

student (if they were not working, only worked up to 20 hours a week during term-time or full-time during student holidays)

self-sufficient person

had indefinite leave to remain (ILR) or indefinite leave to enter (ILE) (under the Immigration Act 1971)

had limited leave to remain on 31 December 2006 that did not place any restrictions on taking employment in the UK, for example, when they:

were given leave to remain under the Highly Skilled Migrant Programme

are the spouse of a British citizen

are the dependent of a work permit holder

have been working in line with their leave (for example, work permit holders or students working less than 20 hours per week) without any breaks in employment that ended on, or after 31 December 2006

You must accept an EU2 national completed 12 months legal employment on the AWS if they met all of the following criteria:

they were in legal employment at the start of the 12 month period - this means they registered their employment on the AWS before they started working with the employer

they were in legal employment at the end of the 12 month period - this means they registered the employer who they were working for at the end of the 12 month period on the AWS, before they started working with them

during the 12 month period, the total number of days they were not working or not in legal employment is not more than 30 days

If an EU2 national’s evidence shows they did not register their employment on the AWS before they started work, none of the employment is considered legal and you must discount any periods of work from the qualifying period.

Accession Worker Scheme: SAWS

The Seasonal Agricultural Workers Scheme (SAWS) was designed to help farmers and growers in the UK recruit low-skilled overseas workers to carry out short term agricultural work.

The SAWS worked on an annual quota basis. Farmers and growers could only recruit a certain number of workers each year. When the quota was full, the SAWS scheme closed for that year.

EU2 nationals had to apply for a SAWS card that gave them permission to work in the UK for a fixed period of time (usually between 5 weeks and 6 months).

If you get a SAWS card, you must make sure the employment details on it match the details on EU2 nationals P60s and payslips for the period of time the SAWS card was valid. If:

it does, the EU2 national will be in legal employment and you can count the employment towards the 5 year qualifying period

does not, the EU2 national will not be in legal employment and you cannot count it towards the 5 year qualifying period

After an EU2 national’s seasonal work ended, they may have returned to their home country, or they may have continued to exercise Treaty rights in the UK. If they stayed in the UK and:

continued to work, you must refer to Treaty rights: worker - you must be aware:

they needed to register their employment on the AWS (unless they were exempt)

if they had already completed 6 months lawful employment under SAWS, they would only need to complete 6 months registered employment on the AWS

stayed in the UK and became a jobseeker, you must refer to Treaty rights: jobseeker

stayed in the UK and became a self-employed person, you must refer to Treaty rights: self-employed person

stayed in the UK and became a self-sufficient person, you must refer to Treaty rights: self-sufficient person

stayed in the UK and became a student, you must refer to Treaty rights: student

returned to their home country but continued to come back to UK every 6 months under the SAWS, we would not consider them to have been exercising Treaty rights (as they are not a resident of the UK)

If you get a SAWS card and are unsure how to deal with it, you must send a guidance query to the Quality and Examination Support team (QuESt).

EU2 national registered on SAWS but cannot supply evidence

If an EEA national tells us they registered on the Seasonal Agricultural Workers Scheme (SAWS) but cannot provide evidence, you must check the UKVI system to see if they did and use their employment evidence to make sure they complied with it.

If there is no record on the UKVI system to show the EEA national registered on the SAWS, you must:

1. Ask them for a signed statement that confirms:

they registered on the SAWS

who they worked for

the start and end date of their employment (we will accept the month and year if they cannot provide the exact date).

2. Decide on a balance of probability if the EEA registered on the SAWS using the employment evidence and signed statement.

Croatian worker: authorisation to work

A transitional arrangement was in place from 1 July 2013 to 30 June 2018 for Croatian nationals who wanted to start work in the UK. This worked in the same way as if they were an EU2 national.

Workers Registration Scheme: family members

An EU8 national’s family member, including if they were non-EEA nationals who were issued with residence document:

did not need to register on the WRS separately (they must still provide evidence to show the EU national exercised Treaty rights for the qualifying period)

can have a Registration Certificate without having to register on the WRS

This means an EU8 national’s family member may not have a WRS card. However, as part of the passport application, they must still supply evidence to show the EU8 national who they depend on, met the WRS conditions.

WRS: how to deal with the Treaty rights application

If an EU8 national was relying on a period of work between 1 May 2004 and 30 April 2009 as part of the qualifying period, you must consider if:

they were exempt from the Workers Registration Scheme (WRS)

the work they did was considered legal work under the WRS (if they were not exempt from the WRS)

This is particularly important as depending on if, and when, an EU8 national is considered to have been in legal employment, it could affect if they exercised Treaty rights as a worker during the qualifying period. For example, you may need to discount periods of employment from the qualifying period if the EU8 national was not exempt from the WRS and they:

were not considered to have been in legal employment

did not register on the WRS at all (as the earliest the qualifying period can start will be 30 April 2009)

If an EU8 national gives us evidence to show they were exempt from the WRS, you must accept they did not need to register on the WRS and you can continue to process the application.

If an EU8 national was not exempt from the WRS, you must ask them for evidence and use UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) systems to help you decide if they met the WRS conditions (by completing 12 months legal employment on the WRS). Evidence you may ask for includes:

Registration Certificates

Accession State WRS Registration Certificates, including employment evidence such as P60s or payslips (so we can check they met the WRS conditions)

You must only accept an EU8 national’s period of work between 1 May 2004 and 30 April 2009 as part of the qualifying period if either of the following apply:

the period of work is considered legal, for example because:

they were issued with a Registration Certificate before the start of the qualifying period

their Accession State WRS Registration Certificates (or information from the UKVI systems) together with P60s and payslips shows they completed 12 months legal employment on the WRS

they registered on the WRS once before the child was born (only in certain cases when we will accept they met they conditions by registering on it once before the child was born)

WRS examples: EU8 national had 1 employer

Below are some examples to show when an EU8 national who had 1 employer would, or would not, have met the conditions of the Workers Registration Scheme (WRS).

Example 1. An EU8 national:

had 1 employer that started on 1 January 2005

applied to register the employment on the WRS on 15 January 2005 and was subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate on 20 January 2005

In this case, the EU8 national completed 12 months legal employment on 1 January 2006 as:

They were legally working at the start of the 12 month period. This is because the first 30 days of employment is considered legal.

They were legally working at the end of the 12 month period. This because they had registered the employer who they were working for at the end of the 12 month period, on the WRS.

They did not have a gap of 30 days or more when they were not in employment or legal employment. This is because there was no gap at all as they:

applied to register their employment on the WRS within 30 days of starting work so their employment continued to be legal after the first 30 days

had no further changes or gaps in employment

For the purpose of Treaty rights passport applications, we can accept periods of employment from 1 January 2005.

Example 2. An EU8 national:

had 1 employer that started on 1 January 2005

applied to register the employment on the WRS on 30 January 2005 and was subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate on 15 February 2005

In this case, the EU8 national completed 12 months legal employment on 1 January 2006 as:

They were legally working at the start of the 12 month period. This is because the first 30 days of employment is considered legal.

They were legally working at the end of the 12 month period. This because they had registered the employer who they were working for at the end of the 12 month period, on the WRS.

They did not have a gap of 30 days or more when they were not in employment or legal employment. There was no gap at all as:

they applied to register on the WRS within 30 days of starting work (even though they were not subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate until 15 February 2005) meaning their employment continued to be legal after the first 30 days

had no further changes in employment

For the purpose of Treaty rights passport applications, we can accept periods of employment from 1 January 2005.

Example 3. An EU8 national:

had 1 employer that started on 1 January 2005

applied to register the employment on the WRS on 15 February 2005 and was subsequently issued with an Accession State WRS Registration Certificate on 20 February 2005

In this case, the EU8 national completed 12 months legal employment on 1 January 2006 as:

They were legally working at the start of the 12 month period. This is because the first 30 days of employment is considered legal.
